faqHeroBody: Everything you need to know about selftest.in
faqAWhatIs1: selftest.in is a lightweight, AI-powered quiz generator designed to help you learn faster. It creates multiple-choice tests on any topic you choose, allowing you to practice
faqAWhatIs2: —one of the most effective study techniques.
faqAIsFree: Yes. selftest.in is currently free to use. We may introduce premium features in the future for power users, but our core mission is to make learning accessible to everyone.
faqQStoreData: Do you store my personal data?
faqAStoreData: We minimize data collection. Your activity, bookmarks, and preferences are cached locally in your browser for offline use. We do not sell your personal data to third parties.
faqASaveQuizzes: Yes. Your quizzes are saved locally on your device for offline support. Clearing browser storage can remove your local history.
faqQAiGeneration: How does the AI generation work?
faqAAiGeneration: We use advanced language models to analyze your topic and generate relevant questions. Our system is guided to create clear stems, plausible distractors, and helpful explanations to keep the learning quality high.
faqQHowManyQuestions: How many questions can I generate at once?
faqAHowManyQuestions: You can choose 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 questions. Longer papers are generated in short batches and checked before they are shown, so a 30-question paper can take a little longer.
faqQBetterQuestions: How do I get better questions?
faqABetterQuestions: Be specific in the planning box: mention the exam, class, chapter and difficulty. 'Class 10 CBSE Physics - light: mirror formula numericals, intermediate' works far better than 'physics'. You can write up to 1000 characters, so add constraints like 'objective only' or 'assertion-reason' when you need them.
faqQWrongAnswer: The AI marked my answer wrong. What should I do?
faqAWrongAnswer: Every paper is checked before it is shown, but a mistake can still slip through. Open Review Answers and use Report question on that item - reports are reviewed. When in doubt, trust your textbook over any AI answer.
faqQDoQuestionsRepeat: Will I see the same questions again?
faqADoQuestionsRepeat: The generator is told which questions you have already seen for that topic and avoids repeating them. If you regenerate the same narrow topic again and again, some overlap is normal - widen the topic or change the difficulty for fresher practice.
faqAExplanations: After submitting a test you can generate an explanation for any question: why the correct option is right and why the others are wrong. Explanations are created on demand, so they need an internet connection.
faqASignIn: No. You can plan, generate and attempt tests without signing in; your history is saved on your device. Signing in with Google is optional and keeps your history, bookmarks and streaks in sync across devices.
faqQDeleteData: How do I delete my data?
faqADeleteData: Remove individual tests from the History page, or clear site data in your browser to wipe local history, bookmarks and preferences. For data linked to a signed-in account, contact us and we will delete it.
faqAOffline: The app and your saved tests are cached, so you can install it and reopen past tests without a connection. Generating new questions and explanations needs internet.
faqALanguages: English and Hindi - for both the interface and the generated papers. Switch the interface language from the header, and choose the paper language separately while planning.
faqADevices: selftest.in is built mobile-first and works in any modern browser. You can also install it from your browser menu (Add to Home Screen) for a full-screen app experience.

blogPost1Point1: Start with a narrow topic and generate a short quiz before reading notes again.
blogPost1Point2: Review mistakes immediately, then generate explanations only for questions you missed or guessed.
blogPost1Point3: Repeat weak topics after a delay so recall gets stronger over time.
blogPost2Point1: Practice with timed, low-stakes quizzes so the exam format feels familiar.
blogPost2Point2: Use shorter sessions when stress is high, then gradually increase question count.
blogPost2Point3: Review errors as feedback, not as a verdict on your preparation.
blogPost3Point1: Review a topic soon after first practice, then extend the gap as scores improve.
blogPost3Point2: Prioritize low-scoring topics instead of repeating what already feels easy.
blogPost3Point3: Use history and results to decide what should come back into the review queue.
blogPost4Point1: Name the exam, chapter, class level, and difficulty in the topic field.
blogPost4Point2: Use optional topic notes for constraints such as formulas, subtopics, or recent syllabus changes.
blogPost4Point3: Save useful quiz presets so you can repeat the same practice pattern quickly.
blogPost1Point4: Spend more time answering than re-reading: five minutes of recall beats twenty minutes of highlighting.
blogPost1Point5: Note which topics you keep missing and bring them back first in your next session.
blogPost2Point4: Breathe slowly for a minute before you start; a steady opening prevents rushed early answers.
blogPost2Point5: Sleep and light exercise do more for exam-day focus than one more late-night revision session.
blogPost3Point4: Keep reviews short and frequent; three 10-minute sessions beat one hour of cramming.
blogPost3Point5: Let accuracy decide the gap: easy topics move further out, weak ones stay close.
blogPost4Point4: Ask for the question types you fear - assertion-reason, matching, numericals - not just easy recall.
blogPost4Point5: Skim the generated paper before attempting it; a good prompt should need almost no edits.
blogPost5Title: A 4-Week Board Exam Revision Plan That Fits Your Syllabus
blogPost5Excerpt: A realistic revision schedule for CBSE, ICSE and state boards: one chapter a day, weekly mixed tests, and a final week for weak topics only.
blogPost5Point1: Split the syllabus into four chunks by weightage: heavy chapters first, easy scoring chapters next, and formula or diagram chapters last.
blogPost5Point2: One chapter a day: generate a short quiz right after reading it, then review only the questions you missed.
blogPost5Point3: Every Sunday, take a mixed quiz from the week's chapters so recall does not depend on the section order.
blogPost5Point4: Keep a one-page error log - chapter, mistake type, the exact correction - and revise the log, not the whole book.
blogPost5Point5: In the final week, stop generating new tests. Retake your three weakest chapters and sleep on time.
blogPost6Title: How to Use Mock Tests for SSC, Banking and Railway Exams
blogPost6Excerpt: Mock tests only help if you review them properly. A repeatable routine for sectional and full-length practice.
blogPost6Point1: Start sectional: 20-25 questions from one subject until accuracy is above your target, then move to full papers.
blogPost6Point2: Simulate the real paper - same question count, difficulty, language and a timer.
blogPost6Point3: Log every mistake under one of four reasons: did not know it, misread it, rushed it, guessed it. Fix the biggest bucket first.
blogPost6Point4: Track accuracy and speed separately. A fast attempt with falling accuracy means slow down, not speed up.
blogPost6Point5: Take one full mock every 2-3 days, and keep the day before the exam light.
blogPost7Title: The 30-Minute Study Block: A Realistic Daily Routine
blogPost7Excerpt: Short, focused blocks beat marathon sessions. How to plan a 30-minute block you can actually repeat every day.
blogPost7Point1: Pick one topic per block. A block with two topics usually finishes neither.
blogPost7Point2: Spend 5 minutes reading, 15 answering questions, and 10 reviewing mistakes.
blogPost7Point3: Finish with a two-line summary in your own words - without copying from your notes.
blogPost7Point4: Same time, same place, every day. Consistency matters more than length.
blogPost7Point5: Two or three solid blocks a day beat a five-hour weekend session you cannot repeat.
blogPost8Title: Wrong Answers Are Data: How to Review Mistakes Properly
blogPost8Excerpt: Every wrong answer tells you exactly what to fix. A simple error-review routine that turns mistakes into marks.
blogPost8Point1: Classify each mistake: concept gap, misread question, calculation slip, or pure guess.
blogPost8Point2: For concept gaps, revisit the source and generate a fresh quiz on just that subtopic.
blogPost8Point3: For misreads, underline the keywords in the question stem before you choose an option.
blogPost8Point4: Re-attempt wrong questions a day later, not immediately - instant retries flatter your memory.
blogPost8Point5: Watch for repeating mistakes. The same error twice means the topic needs a dedicated session.

blogPost6Body1: Most aspirants use mock tests the wrong way: they attempt a paper, check the score, and move on to the next one. The score by itself teaches almost nothing. What improves marks is the review loop after the paper — which questions went wrong, why they went wrong, and what changes in the next attempt. Three numbers matter after every mock: accuracy (what share of attempted questions was correct), speed (how many questions you finish per hour), and the error mix (how many mistakes came from not knowing, misreading, rushing, or guessing). If you track only the score, you will keep repeating the same mistakes with better stamina. If you track all three, every mock makes the next one easier.
blogPost6Body2: Do not start with full-length papers. Start sectional: 20 to 25 questions from one subject until your accuracy crosses your target and stays there for three sessions in a row. For SSC CGL that means separate blocks for reasoning, quantitative aptitude, English and general awareness. For IBPS and SBI PO and clerk papers it means quant, reasoning and English as separate skills, because each has a different error pattern. For RRB NTPC, Group D and ALP, general science and reasoning deserve their own blocks before you mix them with mathematics and current affairs. Sectional practice isolates the weakness; full papers test whether the fix survives under time pressure.
blogPost6Body3: When you move to full mocks, simulate the real paper honestly. Same question count, same difficulty, same language medium, one sitting, a visible timer, no pauses to check a formula mid-paper. One full mock every two to three days is enough for most working aspirants; daily full mocks leave no time for review, which is where the marks actually come from. The day before the real exam should be light — a short sectional revision and an early night beat one more exhausting full paper. Toppers rarely take the most mocks; they take the most reviewed mocks.
blogPost6Body4: Keep an error log with exactly four buckets: did not know it, misread it, rushed it, guessed it. After each mock, assign every wrong answer to one bucket and count. Suppose out of 15 mistakes, 8 are did-not-know (a syllabus gap in modern history and mensuration), 4 are misreads (missed not/except in the stem), 2 are rushed (last-page panic), and 1 is a guess. The fix order is obvious: close the two syllabus gaps first, then add a five-second stem-check habit, then fix pacing. Without buckets, all 15 mistakes feel equally mysterious and nothing gets fixed.
blogPost6Body5: Track accuracy and speed as separate dials, because they fight each other. A faster attempt with falling accuracy means slow down, not speed up — especially with negative marking. SSC papers typically deduct 0.5 per wrong answer and banking papers 0.25, so blind guessing on ten questions costs more than it earns on average. Build a personal skip rule: if you cannot eliminate at least two options within 45 seconds, mark and move on. Return only if time remains. Review sessions should then ask one question per skipped item — was the skip correct, or did you abandon a solvable question too early?
blogPost6Body6: A repeatable weekly routine looks like this: three sectional sessions on weak subjects, one full mock under exam conditions, one dedicated review sitting for the error log, and one light day. Pair it with targeted practice — for example, the SSC CGL, IBPS PO and RRB NTPC practice pages on this site let you generate sectional quizzes and full-length objective papers in English or Hindi in seconds. Take the mock, log the four buckets, regenerate a short quiz on just your weakest unit, and watch that bucket shrink next week. That loop, repeated for six to eight weeks, is the whole game.
blogPost5Body1: Board syllabi feel enormous because students revise chapter by chapter in textbook order instead of by weightage. Start by splitting the syllabus into four chunks: heavy-weightage chapters first, easy scoring chapters next, formula and diagram chapters after that, and everything else last. For CBSE Class 10 and 12 this usually means mathematics chapters like algebra and calculus, science chapters with numericals and diagrams, and social science chapters with repeated previous-year questions go early. ICSE and state boards follow the same logic with slightly different chapter lists — ask your teacher for the last five years of question distribution if you do not have it, because that single page tells you where half your marks live.
blogPost5Body2: Revise one chapter a day with a fixed loop: read the chapter once, generate a short quiz on it immediately, then review only the questions you missed. The quiz matters more than the re-reading — five minutes of recall strengthens memory far more than twenty minutes of highlighting the same page again. Keep each sitting inside a 30-minute block: roughly five minutes reading, fifteen answering, ten reviewing mistakes. Two or three such blocks a day beat a five-hour weekend session you cannot repeat, and the daily rhythm keeps every subject warm at the same time.
blogPost5Body3: Every Sunday, take a mixed quiz drawn from the whole week's chapters instead of revising one chapter again. Mixed practice — psychologists call it interleaving — forces your brain to identify which method a question needs, exactly like the real paper does. A student who practices all chemical reactions together and then all electricity numericals together often freezes when the board paper mixes them. One weekly mixed test of 20 to 25 questions fixes that, and it doubles as your running scorecard: if Sunday accuracy climbs week after week, the plan is working.
blogPost5Body4: Maintain a one-page error log, not a thick notebook. Each row has four entries: the chapter, the mistake type (concept, formula, diagram label, presentation), the exact correction in one line, and the date. Revise the log, not the whole book — ten minutes with the log before each study block prevents the same mark from leaking twice. A typical row reads: Electricity — formula — R = V/I, not I/V — 12 Feb. When a chapter stops appearing in the log for two weeks, it is done; move that time to chapters still bleeding marks.
blogPost5Body5: Science and mathematics need special handling because boards award step marks. For numericals, always write the formula first, substitute with units, then compute — even a wrong final answer earns partial credit for a correct setup. For diagrams, practice labels from memory three times rather than copying once; most diagram marks are lost on two missing labels, not artistic quality. For derivations and proofs, memorize the five key steps as triggers and reconstruct the rest in your own words. Generate assertion-reason and case-based questions deliberately in your quizzes, because those formats cause the most surprises on result day.
blogPost5Body6: In the final week, stop generating new tests and stop opening new chapters. Retake your three weakest chapters, re-attempt your error log end to end, and take at most one light mixed paper early in the week. Sleep on time every night — a rested brain retrieves formulas that a tired brain computed perfectly the evening before. Pack admit card, pens and geometry box the night before, reach early, and read the full paper in the first ten minutes before writing. Boards reward calm, complete attempts far more than brilliant fragments.
blogPost8Body1: A wrong answer feels like a verdict on your preparation, but it is actually the most precise diagnostic you own. A correct answer tells you almost nothing — you might have known it deeply or guessed it luckily. A wrong answer tells you exactly which fact, formula, or reading habit failed, on which topic, under what conditions. Students who treat mistakes as data improve faster than students who treat them as shame, because only the first group opens the mistake back up and studies it. The routine below turns every error into one line of instruction for next week.
blogPost8Body2: Start by classifying each mistake into one of four buckets. A concept gap means the underlying idea was missing — you did not know the rule for image formation or the cause of the revolt. A misread means you knew the concept but answered a different question than asked, usually by missing words like not, except, or always. A calculation slip means the method was right but the arithmetic, units, or sign went wrong halfway. A pure guess means you had no real basis and picked something. Most students discover that only a third of their errors are concept gaps; the rest are reading and execution habits, which are faster to fix.
blogPost8Body3: For concept gaps, go back to the source first and then generate a fresh quiz on just that subtopic — not the whole chapter. Reading the textbook paragraph that contains the exact rule, then answering eight to ten new questions on that narrow idea, closes the gap in one sitting. Resist the urge to re-read the entire chapter; broad revision dilutes the specific correction your brain needs. If the same subtopic produces gaps twice, escalate: watch one focused explainer, make a five-line note in your own words, and schedule that subtopic again after three days.
blogPost8Body4: For misreads, build a physical habit: underline or circle the operative words in the question stem before looking at the options. Words like increases versus decreases, before versus after, and assertion-reason connectors decide the answer before any calculation begins. For calculation slips, separate method from arithmetic — first confirm the formula and setup are right, then recompute slowly with units attached. If you practice with a timer, add a final two-minute sweep reserved only for flagged questions; most slips are caught in that sweep, not during the first pass.
blogPost8Body5: Never re-attempt a wrong question immediately. Instant retries flatter your memory because the question is still warm — of course you get it right thirty seconds later. Wait a day, then re-attempt the same questions cold. What you still miss after a day is your real syllabus; what you now get right was a focus problem, not a knowledge problem. This is the logic behind spaced review queues: the delay is the test. On this site, your history and results already feed a review queue — let accuracy after a gap decide what comes back, not what feels comfortable.
blogPost8Body6: Watch for repeats above everything else. One mistake is an event; the same mistake twice is a pattern, and patterns need dedicated sessions, not more mixed practice. If modern-history dates slip twice, that topic gets its own 30-minute block with a timeline you draw yourself. If sign errors repeat in physics numericals, every practice set for a week starts with a units-and-signs checklist. And one caution about AI-generated practice itself: every paper here is quality-checked before delivery, but a mistake can still slip through. If an explanation contradicts your textbook, trust the textbook and use the report button — it helps the whole pool.
